title: Trump Claims 'Good Talks' With Iran but Threatens Strikes on Pickaxe Mountain if Deal Fails
excerpt: The president said the U.S. has had productive discussions with Tehran while warning he would 'easily' destroy the fortified nuclear site if negotiations collapse.
body:
• President Trump said the U.S. has had "very good talks" with Iran but warned he would destroy Pickaxe Mountain, a fortified nuclear site, if negotiations collapse.
  • Washington suspended a two-week bombing campaign over the weekend, with military commanders advising Trump they were running low on high-value targets.
  • Iran-backed groups launched drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Iraq within hours of the pause, testing the fragile ceasefire.
  • Oman has presented Iran with a Gulf-backed plan to manage the Strait of Hormuz, including voluntary shipping fees, though Washington rejected any toll arrangement.

Trump's Dual Message: Diplomacy and Force

President Donald Trump told Fox News on Tuesday that the United States has been having "very good talks" with Iran, even as he threatened to resume strikes if Tehran does not agree to a deal on its nuclear programme and the Strait of Hormuz.

https://x.com/EricLDaugh/status/2082083467802927269

"I know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe. It's not a big problem," Trump said, referring to a fortified facility buried more than 300 feet beneath Kolang Mountain near the Natanz nuclear complex. "We took out their nuclear sites, and we'll have to take out Pickaxe if we don't make a deal. We don't make a deal, we'll take it out very easily."

"We cannot have them break deals anymore. We have had some very good talks."

— Donald Trump, U.S. President

Trump is due to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House later Tuesday. He dismissed suggestions that Netanyahu was briefing him on Pickaxe Mountain intelligence. "I don't need Bibi to tell me that. Bibi's telling me that because he wants me to stay involved," Trump said.

Why the Bombing Stopped

Washington abruptly suspended its 13-night bombing campaign on Saturday in what Trump described as a diplomatic pause. According to Reuters, General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, had warned the president that the military was running low on interceptor missiles and high-value targets in Iran.

Trump framed the halt differently. "All of the people that deal with Iran asked me: 'Don't fire,'" he told Israeli broadcaster Channel 12. At a rally in Michigan on Monday, he struck a harder tone: "You can't bribe them. You've got to beat them, and we'll beat the hell out of them."

Iran Tests the Ceasefire

Tehran appeared to probe the pause immediately. Saudi Arabia reported shooting down drones aimed at petroleum targets, including in the capital Riyadh. The kingdom said the drones were launched from Iraq by Iran-backed armed groups. Jordan intercepted two drones, and Iraq reported attacks on camps housing Iranian opposition Kurdish forces.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said messages were still being passed through mediators but insisted reports that Iran had requested negotiations were "fabricated." A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran would halt its own attacks as long as Washington's ceasefire continued.

Gulf States Push for a Hormuz Solution

Oman has presented Iran with a Gulf-backed plan to manage the Strait of Hormuz, including collecting voluntary fees from ships using the waterway, according to Reuters. A U.S. official rejected the idea of tolls, reiterating that the strait is an international waterway.

Iran effectively shut the strait to non-Iranian shipping after the U.S. and Israel attacked in February. A deal in June partially reopened it, but the agreement collapsed in early July after Iran fired on ships using an unapproved channel. About a fifth of global oil and LNG flowed through the strait before the war.

What to Watch

The Trump-Netanyahu meeting on Tuesday could shape the next phase of the conflict. Oil markets remain volatile — Brent crude surged above $100 a barrel last week before falling below $92 on Monday on ceasefire hopes. For the millions of Indians living and working across the Gulf, the outcome of these talks carries direct implications for regional stability, energy costs and travel safety.
nri_angle: Escalation or de-escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict directly affects oil prices, travel routes and geopolitical stability for the Indian diaspora across the Gulf.
